The Silk Road took shape around 130 BCE. It began after the Chinese envoy Zhang Qian made his missions west and Han-dynasty China expanded into Central Asia. It then carried trade for about 1,500 years, until the mid-1400s, over more than 6,400 km (4,000 miles) of land routes [1]. Silk, porcelain, tea and spices went west, while horses, camels and gold went east. Ideas travelled too: Buddhism, Christianity and Judaism spread along the routes, and so did inventions like paper and gunpowder [1]. So did disease. The routes may have helped spread the plague behind the Black Death [1]. Overland trade declined after the 15th century as the Ottomans came to control key routes, which pushed Europeans to look for sea routes to Asia [1]. The name itself is modern. The German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen popularized "Seidenstraße" (Silk Road) in 1877 [1]. In 2014, UNESCO listed the Chang'an–Tianshan corridor as a World Heritage Site [1].
